**The problem it solves**

# KeepCloud - The Problem It Solves

Today, users and teams store data across multiple cloud platforms like Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox. 
The experience is fragmented: finding one file often means opening multiple apps, repeating the same search, and manually checking versions or duplicates.

This creates three real problems:
- Productivity loss due to constant context switching between cloud platforms.
- Poor discoverability because each provider has isolated search and metadata.
- Decision delays when users must manually compare documents or verify file relevance.

For students, creators, and fast-moving teams, this leads to missed files, duplicate work, and slower execution.

The problem is even bigger on mobile and chat-first workflows, where users need quick access to files and answers without opening multiple dashboards.

KeepCloud addresses this by unifying multi-cloud files into one intelligent workspace and adding Saarthi AI for natural-language search, summarization, comparison, and recommendations.
It also extends access through a Telegram bot, so users can trigger sync, search files, and get assistant-driven responses directly from chat.
Instead of managing cloud tools, users focus on outcomes.

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I Ran Into

Building a unified experience across Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox was the biggest technical challenge because each provider has different APIs, auth flows, metadata formats, and file-preview behavior.

Key hurdles we faced:
- Standardizing file models and search relevance across multiple cloud providers.
- Handling token lifecycle, secure session flows, and reliable sharelink behavior.
- Keeping Saarthi AI responses fast and useful while indexing diverse file types.
- Making Telegram bot workflows (sync, search, quick assistant actions) consistent with the web app state.

How we solved them:
- Built a normalized backend layer to unify provider data and preview/download endpoints.
- Added secure auth practices, guarded token handling, and robust API fallback logic.
- Introduced caching, background sync, and timeout guards for stable AI workflows.
- Connected Saarthi and Telegram to shared backend services so both channels return consistent results.

This made KeepCloud reliable across web and chat interfaces, even under hackathon time constraints.

---

## ⚡ How It Improves Existing Systems

**Challenges we ran into**

## ⚙️ Challenges I Ran Into

### 🔴 Real-Time Schedule Conflicts

One of the biggest challenges was handling **schedule conflicts in real-time**, especially when multiple admins or coaches were assigning courts and time slots simultaneously.

#### ❌ The Problem
Initially, the system allowed overlapping bookings because:
- Requests were processed independently  
- There was no locking or validation at the database level  
- Concurrent actions led to race conditions  

This resulted in:
- Double-booked courts  
- Confusion for players and coaches  
- Inconsistent schedule data  

---

### 🛠️ How I Solved It

I approached this problem by making the system **conflict-aware and concurrency-safe**:

- **Backend Validation Layer**  
  Added strict checks before confirming any booking to ensure:
  - No overlapping time slots for the same court  
  - No duplicate assignments for a coach or player  

- **Database-Level Constraints**  
  Implemented safeguards (like unique constraints / time-range checks) to prevent invalid entries even under concurrent requests  

- **Optimistic Locking / Transaction Handling**  
  Used transactions to ensure that conflicting operations don’t get committed simultaneously  

- **Improved UI Feedback**  
  Provided real-time error messages if a selected slot was already booked, prompting users to choose another  

---

### ✅ Outcome

- Eliminated double bookings completely  
- Improved system reliability under concurrent usage  
- Made scheduling seamless and predictable for all users  

---

### 💡 Key Learning

This challenge helped me understand the importance of:
- Handling **race conditions in real-world systems**  
- Designing **robust backend validations instead of relying only on frontend checks**  
- Thinking in terms of **scalability and concurrent users**, even for seemingly simple features

**The problem it solves**

**Pollution is everywhere — but no one is accountable for fixing it.**
Every day, millions of people walk past overflowing garbage dumps, polluted water bodies, and toxic air — take out their phone, click a photo, post it on Instagram, and nothing happens. There is no centralized system that connects citizens, communities, and authorities into one action-driven platform.
**The Real Problems ClearCity Solves**
1. Pollution goes unreported or unnoticed
Most people don't know how to formally report pollution to municipal authorities. There is no simple, fast way for a common citizen to raise a complaint that actually reaches the right person.
2. Fake or unverified reports waste authority time
Even when complaints are filed, authorities often ignore them because there is no proof of community validation. A single person's report carries no weight.
3. Zero accountability after a complaint is filed
Once you file a complaint today — it disappears into a black hole. There is no tracking, no deadline, no public pressure. Authorities face no consequences for ignoring reports.
4. No real-time picture of city pollution
Citizens, journalists, and policymakers have no live view of which areas are most polluted right now, which complaints are being resolved, and which are being ignored.

✅ How ClearCity Fixes All of This

- Any citizen can report pollution in 10 seconds using their phone camera — AI automatically analyzes the type and severity, no manual form filling needed
- Community voting validates every report — 5 nearby citizens must confirm it, eliminating fake reports and adding social proof
- Automated SOS alerts send a formal, AI-generated complaint directly to the local Municipal Corporation the moment a report is community-verified — no bureaucracy, no waiting
- Live public map shows every report and its resolution status in real time — creating transparency and public pressure that simply didn't exist before
- The IGNORED label publicly marks complaints that authorities failed to resolve in 7 days — turning inaction into a reputational consequence

**Challenges we ran into**

- During the development of the website, we faced a few technical challenges that required experimentation and problem-solving. One of the main difficulties was integrating the Gemini API to identify pollution from uploaded images. It took several attempts to properly configure the API and design prompts that could accurately detect pollution in different images.

- Another challenge was the map integration. Initially, we planned to use the Google Maps API, but due to configuration and integration issues during development, it was not working smoothly. To overcome this, we switched to Flutter Maps API, which helped us implement the location feature more effectively.
- We also encountered some issues while implementing user authentication with Auth0, especially with configuration and login flow. After debugging and revisiting the documentation, we were able to resolve the issues and successfully implement the authentication system.

These challenges helped us improve our understanding of API integrations and real-world development problem solving.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/smartshield-ai-ca52) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Wahaj-tech/smartShield-AI) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Aegis%20SandBox%20v2.0-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://aegis-sandbox-v.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Intelligent Control Over Encrypted Network Traffic

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![C++](https://img.shields.io/badge/C++-333333?style=flat-square) ![Socket.IO](https://img.shields.io/badge/Socket.IO-333333?style=flat-square) ![SQLite](https://img.shields.io/badge/SQLite-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Modern internet traffic is largely encrypted, which makes it difficult for organizations to understand what services are being accessed on their networks. Traditional filtering systems rely on static blacklists or manual domain rules, which cannot keep up with the rapid emergence of new tools such as AI assistants, social media platforms, or harmful websites. As a result, administrators in environments like exam centers, schools, and workplaces struggle to enforce digital policies or detect misuse of online services in real time. SmartShield addresses this challenge by analyzing network traffic flows and dynamically classifying websites using machine learning and AI-based content understanding, allowing networks to automatically detect and control different categories of internet services even when they are previously unseen.

**Challenges we ran into**

One of the major challenges we faced while developing SmartShield was building a reliable AI-based classification layer for websites. Initially, our system relied on sending extracted HTML content of a website to a large language model to determine its category (such as AI tools, social media, streaming, etc.). However, during testing we observed several limitations. Many modern websites load content dynamically using JavaScript, which means the HTML fetched by the backend often contained very little meaningful text. As a result, the AI model sometimes misclassified websites or returned generic categories. Additionally, calling the LLM for every new domain introduced latency and rate-limit issues.

During the mentoring session, we optimized this AI layer by introducing a layered classification pipeline. Instead of relying solely on the LLM, we first implemented fast heuristic detection using domain patterns and known domain intelligence, followed by improved HTML text extraction (title, meta description, headings, and paragraphs). The LLM is now used only as a fallback for unknown domains. This significantly improved classification accuracy, reduced API usage, and made the system faster and more reliable for real-time traffic monitoring.

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/gigbounty-979e) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Soumyartho/GigBounty.git) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://gig-bounty.vercel.app/) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Diversion%202K26-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://diversion2k26.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Decentralized Micro-Task Bounty Board

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

The **gig economy** is plagued by trust issues, high *intermediary fees, and delayed payments*. Both *web3 businesses* and *individual freelancers* suffer under current centralized models, which often take 20%+ cuts and delay payouts.

**GigBounty** solves this by introducing **decentralized, "trustless" micro-task infrastructure powered by Algorand and AI**. We make freelancing safer and easier by solving core problems across two distinct avenues:

**1. B2C: A Native Web3 Freelance Marketplace**
For everyday users, GigBounty operates as a frictionless marketplace where anyone can connect an Algorand wallet to list or complete work.

**Zero Payment Risk:** We use an Algorand PyTEAL smart contract for escrow. Freelancers know the money is locked on-chain and guaranteed upon completion. Clients know funds are only released when the work is done.

**No Accounts Needed**: We eliminate signups and KYC. Authentication happens seamlessly via Ed25519 cryptographic signatures on the backend, allowing users to collaborate and earn globally with sub-second finality.

**2. B2B: Decentralized Payment Infrastructure**
For businesses, GigBounty acts as a **powerful plugin and API layer**. Companies that have their **own platforms** or internal ecosystems don't need to rebuild trust and payment rails from scratch. They can *integrate the GigBounty plugin to run payments, escrow, and automated release triggers entirely through us*, leveraging our battle-tested Algorand smart contracts under the hood.

**3. Objective, Instant Verification via AI**
To eliminate the subjective quality disputes that ruin freelance relationships across both B2C and B2B channels, we integrated the Google Gemini API (gemini-2.0-flash) as an automated AI Moderator. When a worker submits their Proof of Work, Gemini immediately evaluates the submission against the original task description based on Completeness, Quality, and Authenticity. It generates a strict JSON payload containing a definitive (PASS/FAIL) verdict and its reasoning, allowing funds to be released instantly without humans arguing over subjective details.

**Challenges we ran into**

**Building GigBounty on Algorand came with several real technical hurdles:**

**1. Framer Motion's whileInView race condition** The task card grid was consistently blank on page reload. Root cause: Framer Motion's IntersectionObserver for whileInView doesn't reliably fire for above-the-fold content when once: true is set — elements already on screen when the page loads can get permanently stuck at opacity: 0. Fixed by switching to mount-based animate with per-card staggered delays and removing parent orchestration entirely.

**2. Role persistence tied to a blockchain wallet** Implementing a role system (Bounty Poster vs Acceptor) without traditional auth was non-trivial. Since we use Pera Wallet as the sole identity layer, roles had to be keyed to wallet addresses. The challenge was making role selection feel instant while reliably syncing to the backend. Solved with an optimistic local-first approach — role is written to localStorage immediately on selection, then synced to the backend in the background, so the UI never blocks on a network call.

**3. Algorand testnet transaction verification** Verifying that ALGO payments actually landed on-chain (not just UI state) required integrating the Algorand Indexer. The challenge was handling eventual consistency — the indexer can lag behind the node by several seconds. We implemented a polling mechanism with retry logic to confirm transactions before marking tasks as COMPLETED.

**4. CORS & deployment environment mismatches** The FastAPI backend and React frontend run on different origins. Getting CORS right across local dev, Vercel preview deployments, and production required carefully managing CORS_ORIGINS via environment variables and ensuring Vite's VITE_API_URL was correctly injected at build time.

**5. Escrow wallet security on testnet** Holding ALGO in a centralized escrow wallet for task payouts is a temporary MVP compromise. The real challenge is that any production-grade implementation requires a PyTEAL smart contract to trustlessly hold and release funds — ensuring neither the poster nor the platform can rug the worker. We architected the backend to make this swap straightforward once the contract is deployed.

**Algorand Blockchain Track**

Our project, **GigBounty**, is a *decentralized micro-task marketplace* designed to leverage **Algorand’s** unique high-speed, low-cost infrastructure to solve the campus gig-economy gap.

**1. Leveraging Instant Finality for Micro-Payments**
In a micro-task environment, "time is money." Traditional blockchains with long block times or probabilistic finality ruin the user experience. By building on Algorand, GigBounty offers sub-3.5 second transaction finality, ensuring students receive their ALGO rewards the moment a task is approved—creating a Web2-like "instant pay" experience on a Web3 backbone.

**2. Economic Feasibility via Low Transaction Fees**
For tasks paying 5–20 ALGO, high gas fees are a dealbreaker. Algorand’s fixed, ultra-low transaction fee (0.001 ALGO) allows our platform to facilitate tiny transactions that would be economically impossible on Ethereum or high-cost L2s. This ensures that the maximum value stays in the students' pockets.

**3. Atomic Transfers for Trustless Escrow**
We utilize Algorand’s Atomic Transfers to ensure that the task payment and the platform’s service fee are processed as a single, inseparable unit. This eliminates counterparty risk and ensures that the platform remains sustainable without needing a manual middleman to manage payouts.

**4. Built with the Modern Developer Stack (Puya Python)**
Aligning with Algorand’s 2026 developer initiatives, we have utilized Puya (Algorand Python) to write our smart contracts. This allows us to maintain a unified Python-based backend (FastAPI) and blockchain layer, ensuring high code readability, faster iteration cycles, and a robust security posture.

**5. Real-World Utility & ESG Compliance**
GigBounty focuses on Real-World Assets (RWA)—specifically, human labor. By choosing Algorand, we are building on a Carbon Negative blockchain, which aligns with the ethical and sustainability standards expected by modern university campuses and the 2026 Algorand roadmap.

**Gemini API**

We have used the **Gemini API (gemini-2.0-flash)** in our **AI Verification Module** to act as an automated task moderator.

Specifically, we utilize *Gemini to evaluate* the "**Proof of Work**" submitted by *freelancers* before releasing funds.

Here is how the integration works:

**Contextual Evaluation**: When a freelancer submits proof of completion, our backend sends the original task requirements and the submitted proof link directly to the Gemini model.
**Structured Prompting**: We instruct Gemini to act as an unbiased evaluator, analyzing the submission across three distinct vectors: Completeness, Quality, and Authenticity.
**JSON Response Enforcement**: We use Gemini's responseMimeType: "application/json" configuration to force the model to respond with a strict, machine-readable JSON object.
**Automated Verdicts**: Gemini returns a Float confidence score (0.0 - 1.0), a definitive "PASS" or "FAIL" verdict, and a written reasoning for its decision. The platform then uses this strict formatting to either automatically release funds or flag the submission for dispute.

**Best Beginners' Team**

As a team of "**Vibe Coders**," we represent the next generation of developers who **prioritize AI-driven orchestration** and **rapid prototyping** to solve complex problems. This is our **first** venture into the "**Blockchain Paradigm**," and we have achieved a **full-stack deployment** by:

**Rapid Learning Curve**: Despite having zero prior blockchain experience, we mastered the Algorand ecosystem in under 36 hours by leveraging AlgoKit and AI agents to translate our Python/Web2 expertise into secure smart contracts.

**Agentic Development Workflow**: We utilized a sophisticated "Supervisor" model, using AI (Llama 3 70B & Groq) to generate core logic while we focused on high-level architecture, business monetization, and technical vulnerability auditing.

**End-to-End Execution**: We didn't just build a demo; we built a production-ready workflow—from a React frontend with a custom design system to a FastAPI backend and on-chain escrow mechanisms.

**Problem-First Approach**: Our entry demonstrates that "Beginner" status is an advantage for innovation. We focused on a relatable student problem (campus bounties) and used the most advanced tools available in 2026 to bring a scalable solution to life.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![Flask](https://img.shields.io/badge/Flask-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![Tailwind CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/Tailwind%20CSS-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**The Problem**
Content creators today are trapped in "The Strategic Gap." While AI can help edit or write, it doesn't know why a video succeeds.

1. Data Overload: Creators spend 60% of their time researching trends across TikTok, YouTube, and Google Trends instead of actually filming.

2. Creative Blindness: It’s impossible for a human to objectively know which 30 seconds of a 20-minute raw clip will trigger the current algorithm.

3. Timing Guesswork: Most creators post whenever they finish editing, completely missing the peak engagement windows of their specific global audience.

**The Solution: FrameSync**
FrameSync is the first Content Strategy Engine that bridges the gap between raw creative footage and hard market data. It uses Gemini 1.5 Flash to "see" your content and Snowflake to "know" the market.

1. Automated Hook Discovery
Instead of scrubbing through hours of footage, FrameSync's Gemini-powered Vision Engine identifies "High-Retention" moments—like a perfect badminton smash or a funny reaction—based on visual and emotional cues.

2. Data-Backed Virality
We don't guess hashtags. We query Snowflake’s Data Marketplace to find real-time trending keywords and search volumes. FrameSync then cross-references your video's content with this data to generate titles and tags that are mathematically more likely to rank.

3. Predictive "Best Time" Scheduling
By analyzing millions of data points in Snowflake, FrameSync predicts the Optimal Posting Window for your specific niche. It then uses DigitalOcean background workers to auto-publish your content at that exact moment, ensuring maximum day-one reach.

**Challenges we ran into**

**1. The "Creative Hallucination" Loop**

**The Problem:** During our initial tests, we noticed Gemini 1.5 Flash would occasionally "hallucinate" events in the video. For instance, in a 5-minute badminton clip, it suggested a "viral jump smash" at the 7:45 mark—a timestamp that didn't even exist. It was also inventing "trending keywords" that sounded plausible but weren't backed by our actual data.

**The Fix:** We implemented Strict JSON Schema Grounding. Instead of asking Gemini for general advice, we forced the model to output a specific JSON structure using response_mime_type: "application/json". We also included a System Instruction that strictly forbid it from suggesting any timestamp outside the video's metadata duration. By feeding the Snowflake results into the prompt as "Ground Truth" context, we anchored the AI's creativity to real-world data.

**2. Snowflake Data Latency & Analysis Bottlenecks**
**The Problem:** Our first attempt at querying the Snowflake Data Marketplace was too slow for a real-time "Instant Analysis" feel. The backend was waiting 10–15 seconds for a complex SQL join to finish before it could even talk to Gemini. Furthermore, translating raw search volume numbers into a "Viral Score" that Gemini could understand was mathematically inconsistent.

**The Fix:** We optimized our Snowflake Virtual Warehouse settings, enabling Auto-Scaling and implementing a Caching Layer for common niche searches (like "Badminton" or "Tech"). To solve the analysis issue, we utilized Snowflake Cortex AI functions to pre-process and normalize the trend data inside the warehouse. This meant our backend only received a small, clean "Summary Packet" instead of thousands of rows of raw data, reducing our end-to-end latency by 70%.

**The problem it solves**

## 🚩 The Problem It Solves

Understanding how code actually executes is one of the biggest challenges for beginners and even intermediate programmers. While writing code is straightforward, **visualizing what happens inside the program during execution**—such as variable changes, data structure updates, and control flow—can be difficult.

Traditional learning methods rely on:
- Static code examples
- Console outputs
- Manual debugging
- Complex diagrams drawn by instructors

These methods often fail to clearly demonstrate **step-by-step program behavior**, making concepts like recursion, loops, stacks, queues, and graphs harder to grasp.

Additionally, many existing tools lack:
- Real-time execution visualization
- AI-assisted explanations
- Interactive learning experiences
- Integrated voice guidance for accessibility

---

## 💡 How Ezzzit Solves This

Ezzzit transforms code from **static text into an interactive learning experience** by showing exactly how a program runs step-by-step.

### 🔄 Real-Time Code Execution Visualization
Users can watch their code execute step-by-step with detailed tracing of:
- Variable updates
- Function calls
- Control flow
- Data structure changes

This makes debugging and understanding program logic significantly easier.

---

### 🎨 Interactive Data Structure Visualizations
Instead of imagining how structures work, users can **see them update in real time**.

Supported visualizations include:
- Arrays
- Stacks
- Queues
- Maps / Dictionaries
- Sets
- Graphs
- Matrices

This helps learners build strong mental models of how data structures behave during execution.

---

### 🤖 AI-Powered Code Insights
Using AI-powered analysis, the platform automatically:
- Detects data structures used in the code
- Identifies algorithm patterns
- Explains the logic behind operations
- Provides complexity insights

This helps users understand **not just what the code does, but why it works.**

---

### 📚 Context-Aware Explanations (RAG)
Ezzzit provides detailed explanations using a **retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system** that fetches relevant programming concepts and examples.

Users can choose explanations based on their learning level:
- Beginner
- Medium
- Advanced

This makes the platform suitable for both new learners and experienced developers.

---

### 🎙️ Voice-Based Learning
For accessibility and improved learning experience, explanations can also be **converted into natural voice narration**, allowing users to listen to explanations while observing code execution.

---

## 🎓 What People Can Use It For

Ezzzit can be used in many scenarios:

### 📚 Computer Science Education
Students can visually understand algorithms and data structures instead of memorizing theory.

### 💻 Interview Preparation
Candidates can practice coding problems and clearly see how their solutions execute step-by-step.

### 🐞 Debugging & Code Understanding
Developers can analyze program behavior and quickly identify logical errors.

### 👨‍🏫 Teaching & Demonstrations
Instructors can demonstrate programming concepts interactively in classrooms.

### 🧠 Self-Learning Programming
Anyone learning programming independently can explore how code works internally.

---

## 🚀 Why It Matters

By combining **visualization, AI explanations, and interactive execution**, Ezzzit turns programming education from a passive activity into an **active, exploratory learning experience**.

Instead of asking:

> *“Why does this code work?”*

Users can **see, analyze, and understand the answer in real time.**

**Challenges we ran into**

## ⚙️ Challenges I Ran Into

Building **Ezzzit** involved integrating multiple complex systems such as real-time code execution, trace generation, AI analysis, RAG-based explanations, and interactive visualizations. During development, several technical challenges emerged.

---

## 🐞 Generating Reliable Execution Traces

One of the biggest challenges was **capturing detailed execution traces from user-submitted code** in a way that could power visualizations.

### Problem
Typical code execution engines like **Judge0** only return:
- Program output
- Errors
- Exit status

However, Ezzzit required much deeper insights such as:
- Variable changes at every step
- Function call stack
- Line-by-line execution
- Data structure updates

### Solution
To solve this, I implemented a **custom tracer injection system**.

Before sending the code to Judge0, the backend dynamically **injects tracing logic** into the user’s code. This allows the system to capture:
- Variable states
- Execution steps
- Stack frames

The collected trace data is then returned to the frontend where the **TracePlayer** component replays execution step-by-step.

---

## 🎨 Mapping Raw Trace Data to Visualizations

Another challenge was **converting raw execution traces into meaningful data structure visualizations**.

**The problem it solves**

Today's payment infrastructure is built for yesterday's economy. Independent creators, gig workers, and physical service providers face three major barriers:
* **Cash Flow Lockups:** Service providers suffer from delayed payout cycles (like Net-30 terms or standard T+2 gateway settlements), suffocating the operational cash flow of MSMEs.
* **The Micro-Transaction Barrier:** Charging consumers a tiny amount (like ₹5 or ₹10) is economically unviable due to high flat-rate banking and gateway fees.
* **Compliance Overload:** Independent merchants rarely have the capital to hire dedicated accounting teams, making tax compliance and revenue analysis an overwhelming administrative burden.

### How StreamPay Solves This
StreamPay flips the model by turning money into a flowing utility rather than a static lump-sum transfer.

* **Per-Second Live Streaming Payments:** Money flows securely from the customer's wallet to the merchant's dashboard in real-time, by the second. Users pay precisely for what they consume (e.g., an EV charging for exactly 14 minutes and 20 seconds).
* **Frictionless Wallets:** Customers pre-load their StreamPay wallets seamlessly via UPI. Starting a streaming payment then requires just a single QR scan, completely eliminating checkout drop-off and OTP friction.
* **Embedded AI Financial Advisor:** We integrated an advanced AI (via Gemini) directly beside the merchant's live transaction ledger. It acts as a 24/7 Virtual CFO, allowing merchants to "chat with their data" to instantly answer complex compliance questions regarding Indian GST, TDS, and revenue trend analysis.

**Challenges we ran into**

* **WebSockets & State Race Conditions:** Scanning a QR to stop a stream caused double wallet deductions (front-end local state vs. server-side Socket event). We fixed this by moving all financial math strictly to the Node.js backend and emitting optimistic UI updates only on confirmed `payment:success` events.
* **Database Outage Failover:** When our cloud Postgres DB went offline mid-hackathon, the app crashed. We engineered a custom in-memory fallback (`memStore`) allowing the backend to hot-swap to RAM-based ledger tracking, keeping the core payment flows fully operational without a database.
* **Taming LLM Hallucinations:** Feeding raw transaction data to Gemini initially resulted in hallucinatory tax advice. We successfully guardrailed the AI by strictly typing the ingested JSON ledger history and heavily prompting the system instructions to act purely as an Indian MSME financial advisor.

**Gemini API**

StreamPay directly integrates Gemini into the core financial loop of the platform to solve a very specific problem for Indian MSMEs:

* **Live Data Injection:** We don't just use a standard chat interface. Our backend securely parses the merchant's live, real-time transaction ledger and directly feeds it into the Gemini API payload, allowing true mathematical and contextual analysis of live revenue streams.
* **Specialized Guardrailing:** We heavily prompted the model to act strictly as an **Indian Tax & Financial Advisor**. It rejects casual prompts and focuses entirely on relevant MSME advice (e.g., GST filing, TDS deductions, and HSN codes) based *only* on the injected ledger data.
* **Democratizing Financial Intel:** By embedding Google's AI next to live revenue software, we give independent gig workers and MSMEs the analytical power of a corporate CFO—allowing small businesses to scale confidently without expensive accounting teams.

![HTML](https://img.shields.io/badge/HTML-333333?style=flat-square) ![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![CSS](https://img.shields.io/badge/CSS-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-333333?style=flat-square) ![XGBoost](https://img.shields.io/badge/XGBoost-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

**Problem:**
                Email-based malware attacks are increasingly sophisticated and often bypass traditional signature-based antivirus systems. Most systems lack real-time behavioral monitoring and automated containment, allowing malicious applications to consume system resources, spread across networks, and cause damage before detection.


**The Problem It Solves:**
            Traditional security tools primarily rely on static signature matching, which is ineffective against zero-day attacks, polymorphic malware, and resource-exploiting threats. Additionally, endpoint systems typically operate independently without contributing to shared threat intelligence, resulting in delayed network-wide response and higher breach impact.


**How MailGuardX Addresses This Problem:**
          **MailGuardX** is an intelligent, machine learning–driven email malware detection and containment framework designed to provide real-time protection at the endpoint level while enabling coordinated network defense.

**1. Real-Time Behavioral Monitoring**
The system continuously monitors CPU usage, GPU utilization, network activity, and application-level resource consumption. It differentiates between legitimate, authorized applications and unidentified or suspicious processes.

**2. ML-Based Threat Classification**
When anomalous behavior is detected, relevant email metadata, system usage statistics, IP information, and binary features are extracted and processed using ensemble machine learning models such as XGBoost and Random Forest.

The model performs:
     - Binary classification (Attack / No Attack).
     - Multi-class classification (Type of attack).

**3. Automated Containment:**
- If classified as malicious:
         Internet traffic is temporarily blocked to prevent propagation
         Local antivirus software is automatically triggered
         The attack is contained at the endpoint level
         A detailed incident report is generated for the user
- If no threat is detected, normal operations resume seamlessly.

**4. Distributed Threat Intelligence and Model Retraining**
Attack data is transmitted to a centralized server where:
- Models are continuously retrained using new threat data.
- Other connected systems are alerted.
- Preventive antivirus scans are triggered if similar patterns are detected.

This creates a proactive and adaptive security ecosystem.


**Impact:**
- Faster detection and response to email-based threats.
- Reduced risk of malware spreading within networks.
- Improved detection of zero-day and unknown attacks.
- Automated containment with minimal user intervention.
- Continuous model improvement through data-driven retraining.

**Challenges we ran into**

During the development of MailGuardX, several technical and architectural challenges were encountered, particularly in system-level data access, network monitoring, and automated response integration.

**1. Accessing Device Identifiers and System-Level Data**

- Challenge:
Obtaining access to device-specific identifiers (UIDs), system metrics, and process-level information in a secure and consistent manner across environments was complex. Additionally, transmitting such sensitive data to a centralized system without compromising privacy posed architectural concerns.

- Resolution:
The system was designed to operate primarily at the local endpoint level. All monitoring, classification, and initial threat analysis are performed on the individual machine. Only processed and relevant threat intelligence data is transmitted to the central server for model retraining and network-wide alerting.

- This approach:
       - Reduces privacy risks.
       - Minimizes external exposure of raw system data.
       - Improves detection latency.

**2. Accessing Network Parameters (IP, Ports, Protocols, Timings)**
- Challenge:
Extracting real-time network-level parameters such as IP addresses, ports, protocols, and packet timing data required low-level packet inspection capabilities. Cross-platform compatibility further complicated implementation.

- Resolution:
The solution involved integrating tcpdump for local packet capture and network traffic analysis.

- Implementation considerations:
    - Linux: Installed via apt, dnf, or yum depending on distribution.
    - macOS: Preinstalled or installed via Homebrew.
    - Windows: Integrated using WinDump or Wireshark-compatible packet capture tools.

By leveraging packet capture utilities locally, the system can extract structured network metadata required for feature engineering in the ML model.

**3. Malware Handling and System Compromise Response**

- Challenge:
Detecting a threat is only part of the solution; effective containment and remediation are equally critical. The challenge was designing an automated yet controlled response mechanism without disrupting legitimate processes.

- Resolution:
     - Upon detection of malicious activity:
     - Internet traffic is temporarily restricted to prevent lateral movement.
     - Installed antivirus solutions (e.g., Windows Defender, Norton) are automatically triggered.
     - The affected system enters a containment state.
     - A structured incident report is generated.
     - This ensures that the system transitions from detection to active mitigation
        with minimal manual intervention.

**Key Learning Outcome**
- These challenges led to the adoption of a hybrid architecture combining:
      - Localized endpoint intelligence.
      - Low-level network packet inspection.
      - ML-based classification.
      - Automated containment and distributed retraining.

The result is a secure, scalable, and privacy-aware threat detection framework.

> Zero-knowledge kernel for tabular state transition

![Cryptography](https://img.shields.io/badge/Cryptography-333333?style=flat-square) ![Zero-Knowledge Proofs (ZKPs)](https://img.shields.io/badge/Zero--Knowledge%20Proofs%20(ZKPs)-333333?style=flat-square) ![Rust](https://img.shields.io/badge/Rust-333333?style=flat-square) ![zkvm](https://img.shields.io/badge/zkvm-333333?style=flat-square) ![Plonky3](https://img.shields.io/badge/Plonky3-333333?style=flat-square) ![STARK](https://img.shields.io/badge/STARK-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

# Tabula Thesis

Tabula moves the abstraction boundary from ISA-level execution to
schema-typed state transitions. Memory consistency scales with state
accesses, not total computation.

## 1. The Problem

General-purpose zkVMs (SP1, RISC Zero, etc.) prove machine execution:
a RISC-V program runs, and the prover generates a STARK that the
execution trace is correct. This is general and powerful, but
structurally wasteful for stateful applications.

**Every state access goes through the full ISA pipeline.** A database read
— conceptually, "look up a value by key" — becomes: load address into
register, call memory-read syscall, decode result bytes, store to stack.
Each step is a RISC-V instruction, each instruction is a row in the
execution trace, each row is constrained in the AIR.

**Memory consistency covers everything.** The sorted-memory argument that
ensures "every read returns the last-written value" must cover *all*
memory accesses: stack frames, heap allocations, function arguments,
temporaries — not just application state. The proving cost scales with
total memory operations, most of which are infrastructure.

**Memory is untyped and flat.** The prover sees a byte array. It cannot
exploit the fact that a column contains only u64 values, or that a table
has 50 rows. Type information is lost at the ISA boundary, and with it,
any opportunity for type-aware optimization.

**State root computation is application-level.** zkVMs do not manage
state commitment — they prove execution. When a rollup needs a state
root, the application computes it: hashing leaves, building Merkle
paths, updating the tree — all as RISC-V instructions (or precompiles),
all proven through the ISA. Updating 100 accounts in a depth-20 Merkle
tree requires on the order of 2000 hash invocations, all proven as ISA
execution.

For a batch of 100 balance transfers, the business logic is trivial:
read, compare, subtract, add, write. The proving cost is ISA overhead,
memory consistency over stack+heap+state, and ~2000 hashes for the
state root. The actual application semantics are a small fraction of
the total constraint count.

## 2. The Approach

Computation in ZK has two categories with fundamentally different cost
structures:

- **Stateful** — reads and writes to persistent storage. Expensive because
  of infrastructure: ISA overhead, memory consistency, state root hashing.
- **Stateless** — pure computation: arithmetic, comparisons, hashing.
  Localized: a fixed number of constraints per operation, no memory
  consistency overhead. Cost is predictable and scales with op count
  alone.

General-purpose zkVMs do not distinguish between the two. Both go through
the same ISA trace, paying the same per-instruction overhead. The ISA
abstraction layer artificially equalizes the marginal proving cost of an
arithmetic operation and a state access — a balance comparison and a
database read both become sequences of RISC-V instructions, each
constrained identically in the AIR.

Tabula separates them:

- **State lives in tables** — typed, column-partitioned, key-addressed.
  The IR, commitment scheme, and AIR constraints are co-designed around
  this structure. State root computation is a native protocol concern
  handled by purpose-built AIR chips, not application code proven
  through an ISA.
- **Computation lives in chips** — each operation type (arithmetic,
  hashing, comparison) is constrained by its own AIR chip, connected
  via a LogUp bus protocol. No ISA intermediary.

The rest of this document argues why tables are the right structure for
state, and how the co-design around them enables optimizations that are
impossible in a flat memory model.

## 3. Tables for State

Tables — typed, column-partitioned, key-addressed state — are not an
arbitrary choice. They emerge from the requirements of efficient ZK
proving.

### 3.1 Per-Type Chip Specialization

Each column has a known type from the schema. This lets the constraint
system specialize per type: a Bool column uses 1-FE-wide AIR chips, a
U64 column uses 3-FE-wide chips with limb decomposition, a Bytes32
column uses 8-FE-wide native digest chips. Type information directly
reduces trace width, constraint degree, and lookup table size — each
width class has its own optimized constraint set with no branching and
no dynamic dispatch.

An untyped memory model must either use the widest encoding for all
values, or pay constraint overhead to dispatch on type at runtime.

### 3.2 Per-Column Commitment

Not all state is equal. A 50-row config table and a 10M-row ledger need
different commitment strategies:

- **Small columns:** Sorted Sparse Map Commitment (SSMC) — a sorted list
  with streaming Poseidon. O(n) commitment, no tree overhead.
- **Large columns:** Sparse Merkle Tree (SMT) — O(log n) per access,
  amortized over the batch.

Columns are declared in the schema, so the prover pre-selects the
optimal strategy at compile time. Multiple transactions in a batch that
touch the same column shar

**Challenges we ran into**

## Challenges I ran into

### 1) Removing “RAM consistency checking”

A big hurdle was: **how do we avoid paying a full RAM-consistency argument for everything** (locals, temporaries, repeated reads, last-write tracking), and instead exploit what is **statically knowable at compile time**?

I addressed this by designing the IR around a strict **Normal Form (NF)** and **True SSA**:

* NF makes state access patterns canonical and decidable from the public program structure.
* SSA makes locals wire-like rather than memory-like.
  Together, this removes the need for *intra-transaction* RAM consistency and pushes the remaining consistency problem to the **inter-transaction / batch** layer where it’s smaller and more structured.

### 2) SMT-everywhere was too expensive for small state

Another hurdle was that **SMT openings/updates are overkill when a column is small** (e.g., config tables, compact registries). Using SMT for everything makes the “small state” case pay a huge fixed overhead.

So I introduced **SSMC (Small Sparse Map Commitment)** as an alternative column commitment for small columns, and built a **hybrid commitment model** where each `(table, column)` can use the best strategy for its size/access pattern. This was a meaningful design + implementation lift, because it needed:

* membership / non-membership handling
* update correctness (so the prover can’t silently change unrelated entries)
* clean composition back into a single global state root

### 3) Soundness and crypto engineering were hard

Implementing cryptographic components (hashing/commitments/openings) correctly is full of sharp edges: domain separation, canonical encodings (especially null/absence), update proofs, and “no hidden degrees of freedom” in the witness.

I got through it with:

* lots of iterative testing and refactoring,
* and heavy use of AI coding agents for implementation assistance, code review, and catching consistency issues.

That said, **the current build is hackathon-grade**: it works end-to-end as a prototype, but **soundness/security is not fully finalized**, and there are known issues to harden after the hackathon (more tests, benchmarks, spec/impl alignment, and likely an audit pass).

**Use of AI tools and agents**

## Use of AI tools and agents

I heavily use AI coding agents throughout the project, with **Claude Code** as the primary tool. (Also used Codex when token ran out.)

### How I use agents during development

The codebase is organized as a set of **Rust crates** that are cleanly separated by logical responsibility (core logic, interfaces, utilities, etc.). I also designed the **dependency graph** intentionally so that multiple agents can work in parallel with minimal merge conflicts and clear boundaries.

* **Parallel implementation (2–3 agents):**
  I typically run 2–3 coding agents simultaneously to implement new features, perform refactors, and fix bugs across different crates. Because the modules are well-isolated, each agent can work independently while still aligning with a shared architecture.

* **Review, documentation, and design (1–3 agents):**
  In parallel, I run 1–3 additional agents focused on tasks that are not “writing code,” such as:

  * reviewing the newly written code and suggesting improvements,
  * writing and updating documentation,
  * discussing architecture changes and feature direction with us,
  * exploring new research ideas or alternative designs before implementation.

* **Demo and presentation phase (1–2 agents):**
  In the latter stage of the hackathon, I add 1–2 agents dedicated to shipping a polished demo:

  * building and iterating on the web UI,
  * helping with visual/design choices,
  * drafting the pitch narrative, presentation strategy, slide content, and script.

### How they work together

I treat the agents as a **parallel team** operating over a shared plan and crate-level boundaries. The human role is to **orchestrate**: define scope and priorities, keep the architecture consistent, integrate changes, and verify correctness (tests, code review, and end-to-end validation). This workflow lets me focus on high-leverage decisions and verification while the agents maximize throughput across implementation, review, documentation, and presentation—resulting in significantly higher productivity during the hackathon.

### Meridian
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/meridian-958c) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/meridian-mkt/meridian) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://meridian.directory/) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=azn3OyWYIUI) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Marketplace for acquisitions on Hedera.

![React](https://img.shields.io/badge/React-333333?style=flat-square) ![Go](https://img.shields.io/badge/Go-333333?style=flat-square) ![PostgreSQL](https://img.shields.io/badge/PostgreSQL-333333?style=flat-square) ![hedera](https://img.shields.io/badge/hedera-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Buying or selling an online business today means wiring money to a stranger and hoping they hold up their end. There's no standard process, no neutral custody, and no verifiable record of what was agreed or transferred.

**Meridian solves the trust and coordination problem on both sides of the deal:**

  - Sellers can't verify a buyer has funds before sharing sensitive financials: Meridian gates data room access behind a proof-of-funds check on-chain before any financials are disclosed
  - Buyers have no guarantee the seller will transfer the asset after payment, so funds are held in a 2-of-3 threshold escrow account on Hedera; the seller cannot access them until the buyer confirms delivery and co-signs the release
  - Disputes are handled by a platform operator who holds the third key in the multisig, with full authority to release or refund without either party's co-operation
  - Every milestone from escrow creation, deposit, NFT transfer, to release is written as an immutable HCS topic, giving both parties a tamper-proof audit trail they can point to independently of the platform

**Challenges we ran into**

We ran into some issues with **ScheduleCreateTransaction** and the difference between outer/inner transaction signatures; ended up figuring out that we need to call **ScheduleSignTransaction** a second time, but this took a hilariously long time for us to figure out!

**Use of AI tools and agents**

We used Claude Code and Gemini for speeding up development. The project itself does not rely on any AI tooling.

**New France Village**

This is real economic activity, not yield farming or meme coin gambling. It's two people doing a real transaction (one selling a business they built and one buying it with their capital) settled in USDC on a public ledger with no bank in the middle. 

M&A has always been the domain of lawyers, brokers, and wire transfers. The buyers and sellers on Meridian are small business owners, and Meridian gives them access to the same neutral custody and tamper-proof records that institutions take for granted, through nothing more than a Hedera wallet.

**“No Solidity Allowed” - Hedera SDKs Only**

Meridian is a native Hedera application; every on-chain action goes through the Hedera SDK directly.

Hedera primitives used:
- HTS is the payment and ownership layer. USDC transfers fund the escrow, a non-fungible HTS token (HIP-412) is minted per listing and transferred to the buyer at close. The entire deal settlement (deposit, release, and NFT handover) happens via HTS.
- Threshold accounts are used for escrow logic. Each deal provisions a dedicated Hedera account with a 2-of-3 key list (buyer + seller + platform).
- When the buyer is ready to release funds, the platform creates a Scheduled Transaction for the USDC and adds its signature (1/3). The buyer co-signs via HashPack, hitting the threshold, and the network executes the transfer atomically. 
- HCS provides the audit trail. Every deal gets a dedicated topic with the platform as the sole submit key. Every milestone (ESCROW_CREATED, ESCROW_FUNDED, RELEASE_SCHEDULED, NFT_TRANSFERRED, DEAL_CLOSED) is committed as a timestamped, ordered message independently verifiable on HashScan by either party.
- The Mirror Node API is used throughout for verification: balance checks before scheduling a release, schedule execution status, token association checks, and account public key lookups.

The security model, custody rules, and deal sequencing that would require hundreds of lines of Solidity and an EVM deployment are expressed entirely as Hedera account features and transaction types.

### OpenBar
[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/openbar-9ce1) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/Antoinehrtr/openbar) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/m5M_-tumXbY) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-ETHDenver%202026-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://ethdenver2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Trustless freelance

![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Java](https://img.shields.io/badge/Java-333333?style=flat-square) ![SPRINGBOOT](https://img.shields.io/badge/SPRINGBOOT-333333?style=flat-square) ![Hedera SDK](https://img.shields.io/badge/Hedera%20SDK-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

Freelance platforms like Upwork and Fiverr control a $1.5T market but charge 10–20% in fees, hide how disputes are resolved, and keep all funds and decisions inside a single company. Buyers and freelancers must trust that platform decisions are fair, with no way to audit them. Escrow and dispute logic are opaque and centralized: disputes are decided behind closed doors, with no public record or explanation. Funds sit in platform accounts, so users depend on a single point of trust and can’t move to alternatives without losing history. OpenBar addresses this with transparent, on-chain freelance escrow: low fees (~1%), peer validation with votes logged on Hedera Consensus Service, and payouts handled via Hedera’s native Transfer and Schedule services. Users get verifiable fairness and auditable outcomes instead of trusting a central authority.

**Challenges we ran into**

Wallet-signed transactions. Getting the frontend to sign Hedera transactions was the hardest part. The backend builds transactions with the Java SDK, but the frontend uses WalletConnect and the JS SDK. When passing frozen transaction bytes between SDKs, signTransaction + Transaction.fromBytes() caused INVALID_SIGNATURE because protobuf bytes changed on the way. It took several hours of debugging with StackOverflow and ChatGPT to understand this. The fix was to use signAndExecuteTransaction so the wallet receives raw base64 bytes and submits directly to Hedera, avoiding cross-SDK serialization.
Hedera Consensus Service (HCS). Making HCS work for the audit trail was tricky. Setting up topics, message format, and error handling when publishes fail required a lot of trial and error. We also had to coordinate lifecycle events (TASK_CREATED, VOTE_CAST, DISPUTE_RESOLVED) so the audit trail stays consistent.
Schedule Service for auto-refunds. Wiring Hedera’s Schedule Service for time-based refunds if no freelancer claims in time took careful handling of expiry times, admin keys, and deleting schedules when a job is claimed.
Coordinating three Hedera services. Using Transfer, Schedule, and Consensus together in the right order and error paths, while keeping wallet-signed vs operator-signed transactions clear, added complexity to the flow.
Peer validation flow. Designing the dispute flow so validators (with reputation ≥ 50) vote correctly, reaching quorum, and paying the right party on time required careful state and edge-case handling.

**Use of AI tools and agents**

We used AI tools to build and improve the project:

- UI and layout, Generating and refining React/Tailwind components for the landing page, job views, and modals

- Debugging, Tracking down errors such as cross-SDK transaction signing (Java → JS/WalletConnect), with guidance from AI to locate fixes

- Documentation, Adding Javadoc for backend code, JSDoc for frontend, and improving the README for clarity

- Project structure, Refactoring, extracting shared utilities, and removing dead code with AI help

- Hackathon prep, Using Hedera hackathon skills to evaluate the submission, refine the pitch, and improve the README

**ETHERSPACE**

~~Open~~Bar is built for mainstream adoption. It solves a real problem in the $1.5T freelance market by shifting from platform-controlled escrow to user-owned, transparent flows.
Ownership & identity. Users connect with their own Hedera account (HashPack). They sign escrow and fee payments from their wallet and stay in control of their funds. The platform cannot move money without wallet approval.
Transparency. Votes and outcomes are recorded on Hedera Consensus Service. Anyone can inspect the audit trail on HashScan instead of trusting a private resolution process.
No lock-in. Reputation and workflow are tied to user identities, not a single platform. Users are not locked into a closed database or opaque policies.
Mainstream adoption. The flow matches existing freelance platforms: create a job, fund it, submit work, review. Blockchain details stay in the background. Users only need to connect a wallet; HashPack and WalletConnect handle the rest.
Future expansion. The roadmap includes an HTS governance token for staking and voting on platform rules, giving users ownership of the system itself rather than relying on a central operator.

**On-Chain Automation with Hedera Schedule Service**

~~Open~~Bar uses Hedera Schedule Service for refunds that run automatically on-chain, without manual steps or always-on servers.

Business flow. When a buyer creates a job, they fund escrow in HBAR. If no freelancer claims the job before the deadline, the buyer is refunded automatically. The refund is implemented as a ScheduleCreateTransaction with waitForExpiry=true and the expiry time set to the job deadline. When that time is reached, the refund executes on Hedera without any follow‑up action.

Trustless and resilient. The refund is enforced by Hedera’s network, not by our backend. If our servers are down or offline, the schedule still executes at the configured time. The buyer gets their HBAR back without relying on our availability or honesty.

Lifecycle management. When a freelancer claims the job, the backend cancels the refund schedule via ScheduleDeleteTransaction so the funds stay in escrow. If the job remains unclaimed until the deadline, the schedule runs and refunds the buyer.

Implementation. The refund is a TransferTransaction (operator escrow → buyer) wrapped in a Schedule, with the expiry set from the job’s deadline. This uses Schedule Service for time‑based, conditional payouts in a DeFi-style flow without smart contracts.

**“No Solidity Allowed” - Hedera SDKs Only**

~~Open~~Bar is built entirely with Hedera SDKs and native services. No Solidity, no EVM, and no smart contracts.
Tech stack. Backend uses the Hedera Java SDK (2.67.0) and the frontend uses the JS SDK and @hashgraph/hedera-wallet-connect for HashPack. All Hedera interactions go through the official SDKs.
Native Hedera services.

- Transfer Service, HBAR escrow (buyer → operator), freelancer fee, acceptance payout, dispute payout, and refunds

- Schedule Service, Auto-refunds when jobs expire unclaimed, with schedules cancelled when jobs are claimed

- Consensus Service (HCS), Immutable audit trail: events (TASK_CREATED, TASK_CLAIMED, WORK_DELIVERED, VOTE_CAST, DISPUTE_RESOLVED) are stored on HCS topics and queryable on HashScan

- WalletConnect / HashPack, Users sign escrow and fee transactions via the Hedera ecosystem

Architecture. The backend (Spring Boot, Java 21) builds frozen transactions and returns base64 payloads for the frontend. The frontend forwards these to the wallet’s signAndExecuteTransaction, which signs and submits to Hedera. Operator payouts (releases, refunds, schedule handling) are signed and submitted by the backend.

Why Hedera native only. Transfer, Schedule, and Consensus cover everything needed for escrow: conditional transfers, time-based execution, and an audit trail. This avoids Solidity, EVM gas, and smart contract risk, while still enabling a full freelance escrow flow.

**The problem it solves**

# What Can You Use Baby Shark For?

Baby Shark is a **fully autonomous swap agent**. Once deployed, it requires no human interaction — no approvals, no signing prompts, no babysitting.

## 😴 Set It Once, Trade Forever
Describe your strategy once. Baby Shark runs it indefinitely via a cron agent — executing swaps, managing Permit2 approvals, and broadcasting transactions entirely on its own.

## 🤖 No Confirmation Prompts
Unlike a regular DEX, there's no wallet popup waiting for you to click "confirm." The agent signs and submits on your behalf, end-to-end, while you're completely offline.

## 🛡️ Autonomous Risk Management
Define your stop-loss or exit condition once. The agent monitors prices and pulls the trigger without asking you first — the way a trading bot should work.

## 🔄 Self-Running DCA
Dollar-cost averaging shouldn't require you to show up. Baby Shark executes recurring swaps on schedule with zero human touchpoints between setup and execution.

## 🌐 Always On, Never Waiting for You
No open browser tab. No connected wallet. No active session. The agent lives on a server, watches the market, and acts — whether you're asleep, traveling, or unreachable.

**Challenges we ran into**

# Baby Shark — Technical Challenges & Learnings

Building a fully autonomous on-chain swap agent sounds simple until you're debugging a silent revert at 2am. Here's what we ran into.

---

## 1. 🔐 Permit2 Signature Integration
The Uniswap Trading API requires **EIP-712 signatures over Permit2 data** before a swap can be authorized. Our first swaps reverted silently on-chain because the agent was submitting unsigned or incorrectly structured transactions. We had to decode the raw calldata manually to diagnose the issue, then implement the full Permit2 signing flow — including correctly passing both `signature` and `permitData` together to the `/swap` endpoint.

## 2. 💾 Baseline State Persistence
The agent's trading logic depends on a rolling price baseline to detect swap opportunities. Initially, the baseline was hardcoded and reset on every cron execution — meaning the agent had no memory between runs and couldn't detect meaningful price movement. Solved with **file-based state persistence** via `/tmp/uniswap-baseline.json`, giving the agent continuity across executions.

## 3. ❌ Baseline Poisoning on Failed Transactions
Even after persistence was in place, the baseline was updating regardless of whether the swap actually succeeded on-chain. A reverted transaction would silently shift the baseline, corrupting future decisions. Fixed by **gating baseline updates on `status: success`** — the agent now only learns from confirmed, on-chain-verified outcomes.

## 4. ✅ Wallet Approval Management
The agent's wallet required an ERC-20 approval before Permit2 could spend WETH on its behalf. Without this, every swap attempt failed at the allowance check. Resolved by **auto-granting unlimited Permit2 approval** on agent startup, removing the need for any human approval step and keeping the flow fully autonomous.

## 5. 📏 Minimum Viable Swap Amount
Attempting swaps with `0.00001 WETH` returned no routes from the API — the amount was below the threshold for viable liquidity routing. **Scaled up to `0.0001 WETH`** as the minimum execution size, which resolved routing failures without meaningfully changing the capital footprint.

## 6. ⏱️ Slippage & Deadline Tuning
Initial configuration used `0.5% slippage` and a short deadline — parameters suited for manual, real-time trading. The autonomous agent introduced latency between quote and broadcast that caused consistent deadline expiries and slippage rejections. Relaxed to **5% slippage and a 5-minute deadline**, balancing execution reliability with acceptable price tolerance for the agent's strategy.

## 7. 📦 Uniswap Trading API Returns Unsigned Transactions
A non-obvious but critical constraint: the Uniswap Trading API `/swap` endpoint does **not** broadcast or sign anything — it returns a raw, unsigned `TransactionRequest` object (calldata, gas, value). The agent is fully responsible for signing and broadcasting via its own RPC provider. This meant building a complete signing pipeline into the agent — wallet key management, nonce tracking, gas estimation, and broadcast — with no human in the loop to catch errors before they hit the chain.

## 8. 🤖 LLM Hallucinations in Transaction Construction
Delegating transaction construction to an LLM introduced a class of bugs that don't exist in deterministic code: **confident wrong answers**. We encountered three concrete hallucination failures:

- **Wrong recipient address** — The LLM encoded `0x000...0160` as the swap recipient instead of `ADDRESS_THIS` (`0x000...0002`), sending output tokens to a garbage address with no recovery path.
- **Decimal unit confusion** — The LLM passed `0.000256` as a float for USDC instead of `256000` raw units (6 decimals), resulting in a swap of effectively nothing.
- **Missing slippage protection** — `amountOutMin` was set to `2 wei`, providing zero meaningful protection against price impact.

All three produced transactions that either reverted silently or executed incorrectly on-chain with real funds at stake. The fix was **strict pre-broadcast validation** — every LLM-generated transaction is decoded and checked against expected ranges and known constants before it ever reaches the RPC.

---

## Result

A fully operational autonomous swap agent with:
- ✅ Permit2 EIP-712 integration
- ✅ Persistent rolling baseline across cron runs
- ✅ On-chain verified state updates only
- ✅ Zero human interaction post-deployment
- ✅ Pre-broadcast transaction validation against LLM hallucinations
- ✅ ERC-8021 builder code tracking
- ✅ 100% on-chain execution via Uniswap Trading API on Base

**Use of AI tools and agents**

Baby Shark is built around a **Claude-powered autonomous agent** that acts as the brain of the system — reasoning about market conditions, constructing transactions, and executing swaps without any human interaction.

---

## The Agent: Claude via OpenClaw

The core agent runs on **Claude (claude-haiku-4-5)** orchestrated through **OpenClaw**, a cron-based agent runner. Every scheduled execution, the agent:

1. Fetches a live price quote from the **Uniswap Trading API**
2. Compares it against a persistent baseline stored in `/tmp/uniswap-baseline.json`
3. Decides whether market conditions meet the swap threshold
4. If yes — constructs the full transaction, signs it via Permit2, and broadcasts it on Base

Claude isn't a helper here. It's the decision-maker and the executor.

---

## How the Agent Reasons

The agent is given a **trading skill** — a structured prompt that defines:
- The token pair to monitor (e.g. WMON/USDC)
- The price movement threshold that triggers a swap
- The swap direction and sizing rules
- How to interpret API responses and construct valid calldata

This skill acts as the agent's operating manual. Claude reads market data, applies the rules, and either acts or waits — autonomously, on every cron tick.

---

## The Signing Pipeline

One of the hardest problems was giving the agent the ability to **sign and broadcast transactions without a human wallet**. The pipeline works as follows:

```
Cron trigger
    → Claude evaluates market conditions
    → Calls Uniswap Trading API /quote
    → Calls /swap → receives unsigned TransactionRequest
    → Signs Permit2 EIP-712 message with agent wallet key
    → Constructs final signed transaction
    → Broadcasts via RPC to Base
    → Reads tx receipt → updates baseline only on success
```

The agent wallet is a server-side key. No browser. No MetaMask. No human.

---

## Validation Layer: Catching LLM Hallucinations

Because Claude constructs transaction parameters, we introduced a **pre-broadcast validation layer** to catch hallucinated values before they reach the chain:

- Recipient address checked against known constants (`ADDRESS_THIS`, `MSG_SENDER`)
- `amountIn` validated against expected decimal precision for the token
- `amountOutMin` checked to be non-trivially above zero
- Deadline verified to be in the future

This layer exists specifically because LLMs are confidently wrong in ways that deterministic code never is — and on an immutable chain, there's no undo.

---

## Tools Working Together

| Component | Role |
|---|---|
| **Claude (Haiku 4.5)** | Market reasoning, swap decision, transaction construction |
| **OpenClaw** | Cron-based agent runner, schedules and triggers Claude |
| **Uniswap Trading API** | Quote generation, unsigned transaction building |
| **Trading Skill (prompt)** | Defines strategy rules and operating constraints for the agent |
| **Validation Layer** | Catches LLM hallucinations before broadcast |
| **Agent Wallet (server-side)** | Signs Permit2 and broadcasts — no human needed |
| **Base RPC** | On-chain execution and receipt verification |

**Futurllama**

## AI × DeFi: A New Primitive

Baby Shark isn't a trading bot. It's the first step toward **agentic finance** — where an LLM doesn't just answer questions about markets, it *acts* in them. Autonomously. On-chain. With real money.

This is a new primitive: **intent-driven execution**. You describe what you want in natural language. The agent translates intent into EIP-712 signatures, Permit2 flows, and Universal Router calldata — then broadcasts it while you're completely offline. No human in the loop. No confirmation prompt. Just outcome.

That didn't exist before LLMs were capable enough to reason about structured blockchain data.

---

## Frontier Tech: Where LLMs Meet On-Chain Execution

Most AI x crypto projects stop at the chat interface. Baby Shark goes further — it closes the loop between **reasoning and execution**. The agent doesn't just recommend a trade, it signs it, broadcasts it, and verifies it on-chain.

This exposed genuinely new frontier problems:
- LLMs hallucinating transaction parameters with real financial consequences (wrong recipient addresses, decimal unit confusion, zero slippage protection)
- The need for **pre-broadcast validation layers** to catch confident-but-wrong LLM outputs before they hit an immutable chain
- Stateful agents that need persistent memory across cron executions to make coherent decisions over time

These aren't solved problems. Baby Shark is running experiments at the edge.

---

## Next Gen UX: Trading Without a UI

The current DeFi UX is: open browser, connect wallet, navigate DEX, set slippage, approve token, confirm swap, wait. Repeat.

Baby Shark's UX is: **describe your strategy once, then disappear.**

No app. No dashboard. No wallet popup. The agent handles every step — Permit2 approvals, gas estimation, quote freshness, broadcast — invisibly. This is what next-gen usability looks like when you remove the human from the critical path entirely.

---

## Big Crazy Idea: The Sleeping Investor

The vision behind Baby Shark is that **your capital should work as hard when you're asleep as when you're awake** — without handing it to a custodian or trusting a black-box fund.

Autonomous, non-custodial, LLM-driven execution on Base is the infrastructure that makes that real. Baby Shark is the prototype. The crazy idea is that this becomes the default way people interact with DeFi — not through interfaces, but through agents that understand intent and act on it continuously.

---

**5. Creative Use of API**

• Rolling Baseline Strategy — Adaptive price thresholds that shift after each verified trade (creates market-aware trading logic)
• On-Chain Verification Loop — Only updates baseline after confirming transaction success on-chain (prevents false signals)

[![Devfolio](https://img.shields.io/badge/Devfolio-View%20Project-4B32C3?style=flat-square&logo=devfolio&logoColor=white)](https://devfolio.co/projects/aaroh-f659) [![GitHub](https://img.shields.io/badge/GitHub-Source%20Code-181717?style=flat-square&logo=github&logoColor=white)](https://github.com/mittal-parth/agentic-commerce) [![Demo](https://img.shields.io/badge/Demo-Live-00C853?style=flat-square&logo=googlechrome&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/VIclN1X5rHI?si=SVUUwUDNfEPgXv-V) [![Video](https://img.shields.io/badge/Video-Watch-FF0000?style=flat-square&logo=youtube&logoColor=white)](https://youtu.be/VIclN1X5rHI?si=SVUUwUDNfEPgXv-V) [![Built at](https://img.shields.io/badge/Built%20at-Build%20India:%20Anthropic%20x%20Replit%20x%20Lightspeed%20Hackathon-0052CC?style=flat-square)](https://buildindia2026.devfolio.co) ![Likes](https://img.shields.io/badge/Likes-2-FF6B6B?style=flat-square)

> Enabling agentic commerce at population scale.

![Node.js](https://img.shields.io/badge/Node.js-333333?style=flat-square) ![JavaScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/JavaScript-333333?style=flat-square) ![Python](https://img.shields.io/badge/Python-333333?style=flat-square) ![TypeScript](https://img.shields.io/badge/TypeScript-333333?style=flat-square)

**The problem it solves**

We wanted to build an India-first agentic commerce stack where users can discover, decide, and transact through AI using Google's Universal Commerce Protocol (UCP), and multilingual interactions.

The opportunity is that India has all the primitives needed for agentic commerce - the rise of AI users, the rise of D2C brands, UPI and vernacular users, but lacks the glue that turns this end-to-end experience for both merchants and consumers.

There are two parts to the equation:

**Merchants**

- Need quick visibility into the next frontier of shopping - AI chat interfaces like Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini.
- Lack the expertise to become [UCP](https://developers.googleblog.com/under-the-hood-universal-commerce-protocol-ucp/) complaint and setup the required infra to be visible to millions of users.

**Consumers**
- Users are increasingly searching for products and recommendations on their favourite AI apps. The next step would be the entire checkout process carried out, without leaving the app.
- India represents diversity in languages. A voice-first, multilingual shopping interface is the way forward.

## Features

### Merchants

- Merchants can be visible to the world for agentic commerce by just providing there catalogue and payment information. That's it. All the rest of the heavy lifting is handled by us to be visible on any client. It is fully [UCP compliant](url)https://developers.google.com/merchant/ucp/guides.

### Consumers

- A shopping mcp server which can be added to any chat client (Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT, etc). This takes care of discovering merchants, products, build a cart, generate a UPI payment link and complete the checkout - all without leaving the chat app.
- For an enhanced experience, users can use our own chat client. With this, they can shop in 11+ Indian languages, with either voice or text. The client also supports a richer overall shopping UX.

**Challenges we ran into**

- The biggest challenge was to come up with an executable idea and plan under 7 hours.
- Coming up with a compliant architecture while keeping the UX as simple as possible.
- We had issues while building our own chat client as there are lots of steps involved.

**Hackathon Prizes**

- Used Anthropic's Claude models to build the application.
- Our chat client uses Claude models to handle all the LLM logic.
